prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose early Alzheimer's disease from a family history and a cognitive complaint when memory testing is normal and onset was abrupt.
Do not attribute an abrupt focal cognitive syndrome to stress or anxiety.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor for a strategic infarct syndrome.
Do not anticoagulate without a documented cardioembolic source; anticoagulation has no benefit over aspirin in embolic stroke of undetermined source [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Do not clear her to return to teaching or to drive without formal assessment of the parietal deficits.
required_recommendations: Explain to Mrs Donati and her husband that the syndrome is due to a left angular gyrus infarct six months ago, not Alzheimer disease: memory is normal on formal testing, onset was abrupt and there has been no progression [VASCOG_2014].
Start a single antiplatelet agent (aspirin 75-100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily) for secondary prevention after the ischaemic infarct [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Replace simvastatin 20 mg with a high-intensity statin (e.g. atorvastatin 40-80 mg; LDL 134 mg/dL) to secondary-prevention intensity [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Lower blood pressure gradually to below 130/80 mmHg (currently 146/88 mmHg on nebivolol), checking orthostatic BP at each change [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Advise her not to drive until a formal driving assessment of the parietal deficits, and arrange occupational therapy and an occupational health review before any return to teaching.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role here: the deficit began abruptly, has been stable for six months, and there are no episodes, fluctuation or rapid progression.

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
No parkinsonism, fluctuation, hallucinations or dream enactment: cardiac sympathetic imaging is a Lewy-body test with no question to answer here.
An abrupt deficit that has been stable for six months, not a subacute progressive syndrome: a paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.

A cognitive syndrome can cost a patient her occupation without touching her memory, and the assessment must therefore be functional as well as diagnostic

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Silvia Donati is a 64-year-old primary school teacher who attends with her husband, convinced she has early Alzheimer's disease because her mother was diagnosed at 72. Six months ago, over a single afternoon, she found she could not write the class register or add up marks; the difficulty has not resolved since, and her general practitioner attributed it to stress. She returned to work but has not been able to teach since: she cannot mark arithmetic, mixes up left and right when directing children, and makes letter errors when writing on the board. She has been on sick leave for four months. Her husband has taken over the household accounts because she can no longer add up bills or write cheques correctly. He adds that she loses her place when reading and has twice turned the wrong way when following spoken directions while driving. Her memory for events and conversations is, in his account, essentially normal: she runs the household diary and has not missed an appointment. The change was abrupt and dates to that afternoon; there has been no progression over six months. She has hypertension treated for eight years and takes a statin. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment. She is anxious about the diagnosis and asks directly whether she has her mother's disease.
